content: CD135, also referred to as fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), receptor-type tyrosine-protein kinase FLT3, or fetal liver kinase-2 (Flk2), is a protein encoded by the FLT3 gene in humans. It functions as a cytokine receptor and belongs to the receptor tyrosine kinase class III family. CD135 serves as the receptor for the cytokine FLT3 ligand (FLT3L) and is expressed on the surface of various hematopoietic progenitor cells. The signaling pathway mediated by FLT3 is critical for the normal development of hematopoietic stem cells and progenitor cells. Mutations in the FLT3 gene are among the most frequently observed genetic alterations in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Even in AML patients without FLT3 mutations, elevated levels of wild-type FLT3 have been detected in blast cells, and these high levels are often associated with a poorer prognosis. FLT3 is structurally composed of five extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, an extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, a juxtamembrane domain, and a tyrosine-kinase domain. The tyrosine-kinase domain consists of two lobes connected by a tyrosine-kinase insert. Within the cytoplasm, FLT3 undergoes glycosylation, a process that facilitates its localization to the cell membrane. CD135 is classified as a Class III receptor tyrosine kinase. When FLT3L binds to this receptor, a ternary complex is formed, in which two FLT3 molecules are bridged by a single homodimeric FLT3L molecule. This complex formation brings the intracellular domains of the two FLT3 molecules into close proximity, initiating trans-phosphorylation of the kinase domains. This initial phosphorylation event activates the receptor's intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, which subsequently phosphorylates and activates downstream signaling molecules. These signaling cascades regulate cellular processes such as survival, proliferation, and differentiation. CD135 is particularly important for the development of lymphocytes, including B cells and T cells, but it does not play a significant role in the development of myeloid cells. Two cytokines, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), are known to downregulate FLT3 activity and inhibit FLT3-induced hematopoietic activity. TGF-β, in particular, reduces FLT3 protein levels and counteracts the FLT3L-induced shortening of the G1 phase in the cell cycle of hematopoietic progenitors. CD135 is also a key cell surface marker used to identify specific types of hematopoietic progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Multipotent progenitors (MPP) and common lymphoid progenitors (CLP) express high levels of CD135 on their surface, whereas hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) are CD135-negative. This distinction allows researchers and clinicians to differentiate between HSCs and MPPs during the study of lymphopoiesis and hematopoiesis. CD135 is classified as a proto-oncogene, meaning that mutations in this protein can contribute to the development of cancer. Mutations in the FLT3 receptor are strongly associated with leukemia, particularly acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which arises from malignant transformation of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors. Internal tandem duplications (ITDs) of the FLT3 gene, known as FLT3-ITD mutations, are the most common FLT3 mutations in AML and are associated with a poor prognosis. FLT3 inhibitors have been developed as targeted therapies for AML. Gilteritinib, a dual FLT3-AXL tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is currently undergoing multiple Phase III clinical trials for AML. In 2017, gilteritinib received FDA orphan drug status for AML. Quizartinib (AC220) demonstrated promising results in a Phase II clinical trial for AML patients with FLT3 mutations, particularly those with refractory AML who subsequently underwent stem cell transplantation. Midostaurin was approved by the FDA in April 2017 for the treatment of adult AML patients with oncogenic FLT3 mutations, in combination with chemotherapy. This approval includes the use of a companion diagnostic test, the LeukoStrat CDx FLT3 Mutation Assay, to detect FLT3 mutations in AML patients. Sorafenib has shown significant activity against FLT3-ITD-positive AML, while sunitinib also inhibits FLT3. Lestaurtinib is currently being evaluated in clinical trials. A study published in Nature in April 2012 identified specific DNA mutations that confer resistance to FLT3 inhibitors, providing insights into the development of next-generation inhibitors that could overcome resistance and offer more effective treatment options.
